title: James Nelson Barker, 1784-1858; With a Reprint of His Comedy "Tears and Smiles"
reliability_notes: The first book-length study of Barker and still the standard biographical account, assembling what Musser could find of the dramatist's military service, mayoralty and theatrical career and reprinting his 1808 comedy Tears and Smiles from the early text. Every later bibliographical note on Barker traces back to it, and its dating of the plays by reference to Philadelphia theatre records remains the starting point for work on The Indian Princess and The Tragedy of Superstition. It is a document-driven early twentieth-century study rather than a critical edition: it does not collate all the printings of every play and its attributions need checking against later scholarship.

title: Early American Drama (Penguin Classics)
reliability_notes: A one-volume scholarly selection of plays from the early American national theatre, including Royall Tyler's The Contrast, William Dunlap's Andre and Barker's The Indian Princess (1808), with a general introduction and headnotes supplying performance history and provenance. It is the practical route into Barker's best-known play for teaching and for comparative argument. Because it is a curated selection rather than a collected edition, Barker's other plays are absent and quotations should be checked against the original printings rather than this text.

title: Parson Weems: A Biographical and Critical Study
reliability_notes: A short book-length study of the itinerant Anglican minister and book agent Mason Locke Weems, written by a bibliographer and book collector who was then building the first serious record of Weems's printing and peddling career. It remains the earliest sustained attempt to separate the historical Weems from the sentimental 'Parson Weems' myth and is still cited for the chronology of his editions. It is an early twentieth-century bibliographical pamphlet rather than a modern academic biography: its conclusions rest on the trade evidence available in 1911, and Skeel's documentary volumes of 1929 supersede parts of it.

title: Mason Locke Weems, His Works and Ways (3 volumes)
reliability_notes: The documentary foundation for all Weems scholarship: volume one completes the bibliography of his editions left unfinished by Paul Leicester Ford, and volumes two and three print his letters from 1784 to 1825, much of it from family papers. It is the authority for the number, date and imprint of the many issues of the Life of Washington and for the details of his book-agenting routes. It is a privately printed limited edition, so it is unevenly held by research libraries, and its dating of individual letters has been qualified by later work on the Mathew Carey papers.

title: Hope Leslie: Or, Early Times in the Massachusetts (American Women Writers series)
reliability_notes: The scholarly text that brought Sedgwick's 1827 novel back into circulation, in the Rutgers American Women Writers series, with Kelley's introduction and explanatory notes situating the novel in its Puritan-source, anti-Indian-policy and gender-politics contexts. It is the citation standard for Hope Leslie and the edition that made the novel recoverable for undergraduate and graduate teaching alike. It reprints the 1827 three-decker in single-volume form with modernized punctuation and spelling in places, so quotations used in textual argument should be checked against the 1827 first edition.

title: The Power of Her Sympathy: The Autobiography and Journal of Catharine Maria Sedgwick
reliability_notes: A documentary edition of Sedgwick's memoir and journals drawn from the family papers, with an introduction and annotation that identify the large cast of correspondents and events she names. It is the principal source for Sedgwick's own account of her childhood, her evangelical conversion and its undoing, her family's politics and the making of her novels. The autobiography is a retrospective written decades after the events and the journal is fragmentary and partly in cipher, so its dates and self-portrait must be cross-checked with the surviving correspondence.

title: The Life and Writings of Hugh Henry Brackenridge
reliability_notes: Still the fullest biographical and bibliographical study of Brackenridge, tracing the Scottish-born novelist's career as Presbyterian chaplain, lawyer, editor of the Pittsburgh Gazette and playwright, and attempting a chronology of Modern Chivalry's serial parts. Its account of the composition and issue dates of the Chivalry parts is the basis most later scholars work from or against. It is a 1932 literary-biographical study, so its moral and political judgments on Brackenridge are dated, and its publication data should be verified against the imprints themselves and against later work on his Lancaster and Pittsburgh printing.

title: Modern Chivalry (American Fiction Series)
reliability_notes: The reading edition of Brackenridge's novel, assembled by Newlin from the parts published between 1792 and 1815 and supplied with his introduction and notes; it is the version normally cited and taught. Because Modern Chivalry grew by instalments and was twice re-arranged by its author, Newlin's consolidation into one continuous text is an editorial construction rather than any single historically printed book. Researchers working on its politics or its textual history must check the individual part editions, since readings, sequence and the late-volume satires differ from this text.

title: Timothy Dwight, 1752-1817: A Biography
reliability_notes: A full-length documentary biography (403 pages) of Yale's president, working through the manuscripts and the family papers to reconstruct Dwight's presidency, his controversy with the Democratic-Republicans, the student declamations and the revival of 1802. It remains the most detailed narrative of his public career and the usual source for dates and quotations from his Yale years. It is a mid-century political and institutional biography rather than a literary study: its reading of the poetry and the Travels is thin by later standards, and its Protestant-elite sympathies should be weighed against Silverman's account.

title: Timothy Dwight (Twayne's United States Authors Series, No. 145)
reliability_notes: A concise critical study in the standard Twayne authors series, analyzing Dwight's thinking on the major issues of his time through his principal writings, from Greenfield Hill and the Travels to the theology and the Yale addresses. It is the dependable short introduction and, being by a scholar of American literature, stronger on the writings than Cunningham's biography. It is a short monograph of some 170 pages that assumes the older edition it cites, so details of text and date should be verified against the Travels edition and the original imprints.

title: Researches in the South of Ireland (CELT: Corpus of Electronic Texts)
author_or_editor: Thomas Crofton Croker (author); Ruth Murphy and Beatrix Färber (CELT editors)
reliability_notes: A machine-readable scholarly text of Croker's Researches in the South of Ireland (London: John Murray, 1824), prepared by CELT at University College Cork from the printed original, and the practical way to search and quote the work, which is otherwise a rare three-decker antiquarian survey. It documents Cork, Kerry and Waterford scenery, architecture, pilgrim patterns, the keen and peasant superstition, and is the founding text of Irish folklore studies. CELT transcribes the 1824 text without modern editorial annotation, so its topographical identifications, its dating of the ballads and its claims about 'unperverted' Celtic tradition must be checked against later archaeology and against Croker's known practice of borrowing from informants such as Peter Hardiman without credit.

title: Fairy Legends and Traditions of the South of Ireland, with a Short Memoir of the Author by His Son
reliability_notes: The collected edition of Croker's Fairy Legends (first published 1825-1828), furnished with the family memoir by his son T. F. Dillon Croker, the usual source for the tales together with the biographical details of Cork, London and the Murray correspondence. It is posthumous and lightly edited: the memoir is apologising and selective, and it reproduces the tales as Croker last revised them rather than in their earlier state. Anyone working on the tales' origins should compare the 1825 and 1828 volumes and the German and Irish analogues, since the notes here do not distinguish Croker's own composition from what he took from Hardiman and other collectors.

title: Journal of a Residence in Chile During the Year 1822, and a Voyage from Chile to Brazil in 1823
reliability_notes: Hayward's scholarly edition of Maria Graham's Chile journal, with introduction and notes that establish the documentary, botanical and political context of her stay in the newly independent republic and her account of the 1822 earthquake. It is the standard text for citing Graham in Latin American travel-writing and science-history work, and it restores her authorial role against the older assumption that her husband wrote the observations. It reprints the 1824 narrative, so passages Graham cut or softened for publication, and her relations with the British diplomatic mission, need checking against her unpublished letters and against the companion Voyage to Brazil volume.

title: Maria Graham's Journal of a Voyage to Brazil (Writing Travel)
reliability_notes: An annotated scholarly edition of Graham's 1824 Brazil journal in Broadview's Writing Travel series, with introduction and notes attending to her drawing and plant collecting, her contacts with naturalists, and her remarks on slavery and on the Portuguese court in Rio. It is the most accessible current text and the best starting point for the Brazilian narrative. Because it edits a single travel volume apart from the Chile journal and the earlier published Letters on India, comparative quotations should be checked against those originals, and its modernized text should not be used for bibliographical collation.

title: The Boyne Water: A Tale (3 volumes)
reliability_notes: A facsimile reprint, in three volumes, of Banim's 1826 historical novel about the Williamite war in Ireland, the most ambitious of his Irish tales and the one usually treated as his major work. It is the practical way to read the triple-decker as it first appeared, since original copies of the three volumes are scarce. The reprint carries no new editorial apparatus, so its prefatory matter, dedication and publisher's advertisements must be read as 1826 trade material, and its political framing should be compared with the O'Hara tales and with the account of the novel's authorship given in Murray's 1857 Life.

title: The Life of John Banim, the Irish Novelist
reliability_notes: The contemporary biography of John Banim, compiled with the cooperation of his brother Michael and containing extracts from Banim's correspondence and papers; it is the origin of almost every fact later repeated about the brothers' Kilkenny childhood, London struggle and John's final blindness and death. It is indispensable but partisan: Murray wrote to secure Michael's share of the family reputation and to defend the Catholic politics of the tales, so its dating of the collaborations and its division of labour between the brothers need testing against the printed texts and against Michael's own later account.

title: Dictionary of Irish Biography: From the Earliest Times to the Year 2002 (9 volumes)
publisher: Cambridge University Press in collaboration with the Royal Irish Academy
reliability_notes: The standard scholarly biographical dictionary for Ireland, whose signed entry on John Banim supersedes the Victorian account and sorts out the joint authorship of the O'Hara tales with documentary evidence. It is the right first stop for dates, family, patronage and publication history, and each entry gives its own sources. Entries are short and selectively referenced, so a researcher following a claim about the Banims' authorship or their finances must go on to the cited archival material rather than treat the dictionary as the last word.

title: Freedom's Journal (New York, 1827-1829): Digitised Run, Chronicling America
author_or_editor: Samuel E. Cornish and John Brown Russwurm (editors and proprietors); Library of Congress (digitising publisher)
reliability_notes: The digitised run of the first African American-owned newspaper in the United States, weekly in New York from its first number on 16 March 1827 until it ceased in 1829, and the primary text for the editorial work of Cornish and Russwurm: the opening address 'To Our Customers Respecting Ourselves', the reports of African American societies, schools and ordinations, the reprinted abolitionist correspondence, and the debate over colonization. It is complete, searchable and free, which no microfilm set is. The file survives imperfectly and the editors divided during the run - Cornish resigned as co-editor in the issue of 14 September 1827, leaving Russwurm sole editor - so every item must be dated and attributed with that division in view rather than treated as jointly written.

title: The Rights of All (New York, 1829): Digitised Run, Chronicling America
author_or_editor: Samuel E. Cornish (editor and publisher); Library of Congress (digitising publisher)
reliability_notes: Cornish's successor to Freedom's Journal, printed in New York from May 1829 after he reclaimed the editorial chair, and the main body of his own mature journalism: the attacks on the American Colonization Society, the reports of black state conventions, and the arguments for manual-labour schools and temperance. It is the only convenient access to a sheet that survives in very few libraries. The run is short and partly incomplete, its imprint gives Cornish alone, and its columns often republish other people's letters, so quotations need to be checked for their original author and date before being credited to Cornish himself.

title: The Struggles of John Brown Russwurm: The Life and Writings of a Pan-Africanist Pioneer, 1799-1851
reliability_notes: A scholarly biography that also collects and prints Russwurm's surviving writings, following him from Jamaica and Maine to the founding of Freedom's Journal and his emigration to Liberia; it is the current standard account and the best-edited route into a scattered textual record. It deliberately rehabilitates Russwurm's controversial turn to colonization and his abandonment of Cornish's anti-missionary line, so its sympathetic readings should be tested against the newspaper texts themselves and against the black convention movement it necessarily treats at second hand.

title: The Complete Works of Walter Savage Landor (16 volumes)
author_or_editor: T. Earle Welby and Stephen Wheeler (editors)
reliability_notes: The first collected edition of Landor, complete in sixteen volumes published between 1927 and 1936, gathering the Imaginary Conversations in their several series, the prose translations, the Greek and Latin writings and the poems; volumes thirteen to sixteen were reissued separately as The Poetical Works by the Clarendon Press in 1937. It is still the default citation for a Landor text that has no modern complete edition. It is not a scholarly textual edition: it does not date or collate the original printings, it follows Victorian ordering rather than composition, and Landor's own revisions between editions have to be recovered from the first issues themselves.

title: Landor's Cleanness: A Study of Walter Savage Landor
reliability_notes: The first monograph devoted to Landor in some fifty years, reading the whole surviving range - the conversations, the epigrams and idylls, the Latin and Greek writing, the political tracts - against the critical neglect of Landor's later career. It is the natural starting point for an argument about Landor's place in Romantic letters and it challenges the Saintsbury-derived view of him as merely a stylist. It is a single-author critical study, not an edition, so quotations and publication dates it uses must be taken from the Welby and Wheeler collection or from the first editions rather than from this book.

title: Rural Rides (Penguin English Library)
reliability_notes: The standard twentieth-century reading text of Cobbett's Rural Rides, edited and introduced by George Woodcock from the 1830 collected edition, with a Penguin English Library impression in 1967 later reprinted with an index. Its introduction is a shrewd account of Cobbett as a radical agrarian journalist and it made the book affordable to several generations of students. It abridges Cobbett's serial rides and regularizes his spelling and capitalisation, so a scholar using his phrasing, his political allusions or the sequencing of the rides must consult the Political Register instalments or the 1830 two-volume original.

title: William Cobbett: The Politics of Style (Cambridge Studies in Romanticism)
reliability_notes: A literary study of Cobbett's writing as political argument, reading the Register, the grammars, the rural journalism and the polemic against 'puffery' in terms of his deliberate stylistic theory, and the book that moved Cobbett back into Romantic-period literary history. It is strong on style, register and rhetorical self-fashioning, and it is the usual guide for anyone arguing about Cobbett's prose. Its account is organized around Cobbett's own conception of writing, so economic and popular-reading evidence, and the reception of the Register outside the radical public, need to be checked against the historians' accounts.

title: The Principles of Political Economy: With a Sketch of the Rise and Progress of the Science (Cambridge Library Collection)
reliability_notes: A facsimile reprint by Cambridge University Press, in its Cambridge Library Collection series, of the first edition of McCulloch's treatise (Edinburgh: Archibald Constable and Co., 1825), the book that made him the leading expositor of Ricardo and established him as professor of political economy at London. It is the work through which 'Ricardian' economics reached Victorian readers and undergraduates, and it is the correct text for citing his doctrine of rent, wages and profit as first stated. Heavily revised in the second to fifth editions (the last of 1864), so the text is not stable: quotations and argument must be pinned to the edition used, and his later statistical and colonial writing sits outside this book.

title: The Literature of Political Economy: A Classified Catalogue of Select Publications in the Different Departments of That Science, with Historical, Critical and Biographical Notices (Cambridge Library Collection)
reliability_notes: Reprinted by Cambridge University Press from the 1845 first edition, this is McCulloch's great bibliography of the whole printed literature of political economy, arranged by department and supplied with historical, critical and biographical notices; it is also the fullest surviving statement of his own reading and of the canon he wanted the science to have. It remains a standard tool for tracing which tracts, pamphlets and books were actually available to nineteenth-century economists, and its library sale catalogues give prices and copies. Its attributions and dates are those of a nineteenth-century collector and its judgments are frequently dismissive, so each entry should be checked against modern bibliographies before it is quoted as fact.
